r.t: This doc will explain my conservative interpretation of the 17 Poker FSIQ feat. This is not necessarily the only possible interpretation, but it is one that avoids wank the most.

The game 17 Poker follows the rules of normal poker for the most part except a few things. It has 17 cards total instead of a full deck. Secondly it includes a Joker that can take the place of any card on the deck. So if you have a Joker in your hand, you can use it as any of the remaining 16 cards to get the best possible hand from the cards given to you. The other 16 cards include 4 Aces, 4 Jacks, 4 Queens, and 4 Kings. The hierarchy of the hands is as follows:
The dealer takes out a fresh deck each round.
The dealer asks both players how many cards from the top they wish to cut
Then the betting starts. The exact rules of betting aren’t really relevant here.
Akiyama notices the dealer’s perfect shuffle during the mock game
Akiyama notices Kikuchi’s strategy during the 4th hand of the actual hand

Likely at the start of hand 5, he realized that the dealer uses a new deck each round. He considered the possibility that every deck has the same order of cards. Akiyama’s theory is confirmed by the 6th hand.
He then states that that’s when he came up with his idea of locating the position of every card in the deck. Akiyama confirms the exact starting order by the 8th hand.
He explains how the perfect shuffle arranges the deck each time

By the 8th shuffle you go back to where you started. Akiyama also states that his goal in the 8th round was to confirm the starting order of the cards. He asked to exchange 5 cards which allowed him to know 10 cards in the deck.

With the knowledge of the patterns of perfect shuffle and the starting order of the cards, Akiyama was able to manipulate the dealer and the game in a way that he’d always have 4 of a kind, a hand that Kikuchi could never beat. With all that out of the way, let’s move on to the interpretation.
*This doc’s purpose is to calculate the “Low End Interpretation”. It also calculates the “Mid End Interpretation” to allow people to make informed choices.

The highest end assumes that Akiyama shuffles the cards in his head every time the dealer does. This is about 17 cards shuffled every second or so. So it comes out to 8.5-17 operations per second. However this is a complete wank and directly contradicts Akiyama’s strategy. Akiyama stated that he calculated the best number of shuffles and THEN manipulated the dealer to force that number of shuffles. So if he only figured out the order after the 8th hand ended, and manipulated the dealer before the 9th hand started, the dealer didn’t have the opportunity to shuffle in front of him which eliminates the possibility of him matching the dealer’s speed of shuffling.
Mid End Interpretation (Generous but not incorrect)

This is the mid end interpretation of the feat. In this we assume that Akiyama shuffled the cards in his head after the 8th hand ended and before the 9th hand started. Akiyama couldn’t have known the position of any card in the starting order before the 8th hand since the dealer still used Hindu shuffle before. Thus, we know for a fact that Akiyama confirmed the order during the 8th hand itself. This interpretation assumes that after knowing the exact starting order, Akiyama runs the 8 shuffles in his head using the starting order and decides the number of shuffles necessary for him to win. Between him revealing the 8th hand and him interrupting the dealer for the first time in the 9th hand (he asks the dealer to shuffle one more time to get his desired order) there were around 332 words spoken by all the characters.

I will calculate the WMI of Akiyama in the Low End Interpretation because WMI should not be affected by the timeframe and should be the same in all interpretations.

This interpretation involves the assumption that Akiyama formed his strategy starting the 5 minute break offered after the 6th hand. This is because Akiyama stated that he confirmed Kikuchi’s strategy in the 6th hand as shown above. Right after he states the following:

So it is my reasoning that right after confirming Kikuchi’s strategy, Akiyama started formulating his own strategy. And then he made all the necessary calculations in his head during all the conversation that Nao had with the other team. We know Akiyama wasn’t holding a pen and paper the entire time. Also he technically had time starting from the break, until he interrupted the dealer in the 9th round to calculate all the patterns on the perfect shuffle. However a possible rebuttal to this explanation can be “How can Akiyama run all the patterns in his head if he doesn’t even know the starting order of the deck.” However this is logically possible and actually supported by Akiyama’s explanation. Akiyama knew that the dealer uses a new deck every time as early as the fifth hand. So by the 6th hand he definitely had the logic ready. All he needed were placeholders of all the cards to run in his head and identify the pattern. Here is a visual representation of this in an Excel sheet.

Here I used A, B, C, D as placeholders for the cards in the deck. Here A would be the Joker in the actual order. You can see that we can actually trace A to Joker’s position in Akiyama’s explanation as well. And by the 8th shuffle you can see that the placeholders are in alphabetical order as Akiyama said. So there is no actual need to know the starting order to know the pattern after each shuffle. After creating this table in his head, Akiyama simply needs to replace the placeholders with the actual cards as he finds out their order one by one in the 8th hand. Let me make the table with the actual starting order

I used formulae in this Excel file. For the first 8 positions in a deck, a perfect shuffle changes its position to double its initial rank in the deck. For example the 1st card becomes 2nd, 2nd becomes 4th, 3rd becomes 6th, and so on. The 17th card does not change its position at all. The cards starting from 9th occupy the remaining odd places in order. So 9th becomes 1st, 10th becomes 3rd, 11th becomes 5th, and so on. Once you understand the logic which Akiyama must have caught on pretty early on, it is very predictable. Though I need an Excel sheet or a paper to follow it for 8 shuffles and Akiyama can do it in his mind.

After he had formulated the table in his mind, all he needed to do was to look at the pattern of the shifts in Joker’s position.This way he was able to find the best possible number of shuffles for him. So he essentially had 5 mins + 7th round + 8th round + some of 9th round to calculate the entire table and the best possible pattern for his strategy.

A given timeframe of 5 minutes makes it easy for me to do this calculation. Of course Akiyama couldn’t have made all the calculations during the 5 minute break since he didn’t even know the starting order yet. But we can infer from above that whatever the timeframe is will be more than 5 minutes. So we can at least calculate a high end for Akiyama in this methodology.
Using this we can assume Akiyama had plenty of time to work through the calculations at average processing speeds.

This shows high detail oriented VSI. Also if we consider the Low End Interpretation of the feat, the Excel format also gives us the same ballpark in terms of VSI where each placeholder represents one card.

Obviously the level of detail in visualization is impressive in the case of Akiyama, but we can’t really quantify that. Therefore we need to compare it with other feats or characters on a case by case basis. However building a sequence or table in one’s head and manipulating the elements to match the shuffle patterns requires Visual Reasoning. Simon Reinhard as mentioned above is the world record holder in forward digit span. He is stated to be a user of the method of loci, a mnemonic technique which uses visualization to remember things. The Memory Palace technique falls under this. Which is why it is not unreasonable to assume that Akiyama would have had to use some sort of method of loci to remember the 136 card shuffle positions. Which further supports the VSI component of this feat.
